Overview/Deed amounts

Paper 02 · Deed amounts

When a Deed Is Not a Market Sale

Foreclosure Transfers, Statutory Consideration, and Repeat-Sales House-Price Measurement

By Pablo LoschiPublic version 1.0.4Document review reported

The question

When a lender takes title through foreclosure or a deed in lieu, New York transfer-tax rules can base the recorded consideration on a bid, judgment or discharged debt rather than a negotiated price. Should that amount enter a house-price index as if it were a sale price?

The paper classifies such deeds by their parties across every deed recorded in Manhattan, the Bronx, Brooklyn and Queens from 2003 to 2025, and measures what they do to a standard repeat-sales index.

Results

  • 16,655deeds labelled as legal-rule transfers among 1.47 million, 2003–2025
  • 70%of their amounts carry cents, against 6% of ordinary sales; yet conventional screens keep them
  • 94–95%of those recorded in 2016–25 appear in the city's public sales file at the recorded amount
  • 0.6log points: difference in the peak-to-trough decline (interval −3.0 to +1.2). The path, not the total, changes
  • 99.3%of flagged deeds are read as non-market, among resolved cases in a document review of 400 sampled deeds; the classifier finds 96.6% of foreclosure transfers

Why it matters

  • Repeat-sales indices, hedonic models and local price series built from public deed records inherit these amounts unless deeds are classified by their parties: the document type does not distinguish them.
  • The distortion is to timing: the raw index falls less into 2009–10 and more into 2011–12, which matters for short-window returns and borough comparisons.
  • Dropping contaminated pairs and bridging across them answer different questions; the choice moves the crisis decline by about five log points and should be made explicitly.
  • The classifier is released as a free, dependency-light Python module.
Index buildersUrban economistsUsers of ACRIS and DOF sales data

Validation status

Version 1.0.3 reports a document review of a stratified probability sample of 400 deeds. The original protocol called for two human readers; this version uses AI instead. ChatGPT read every deed image, and Claude then checked each reading against the city's open data and the protocol's rules and sent doubtful ones back. The rates below measure agreement with those readings, not accuracy against a verified record. Among resolved deeds, 99.3% of the deeds the classifier flags are read as non-market (95% interval 97.8–100%). It finds 96.6% of foreclosure transfers (93.4–99.8%), but only about half of all non-price transfers, because it does not look for sales between relatives. 84 deeds stay unresolved, most of them auction purchases whose deed images cannot show whether bidding was competitive.

Version 1.0.4 checks that the index result does not rest on doubtful cases. Dropping only the narrowest set, referee's deeds to lenders with an amount in cents and no securitization-type buyer, still moves the 2010Q3 house index by 2.6 log points (interval 1.8–3.7), about a third of the flagged deeds. The largest of 200 matched placebo draws is 1.2. Every narrower and broader definition beats all of its own placebo draws. These are subsets of the same classifier, not an independent check.

The answer key was opened only after the readings were locked, and it matches the hash published before the review began. The readings, the revision log and the key are in the version 1.0.3 and later archives.
